summary: A 1977 note warning designers of Telnet options about a possible pitfall involving the Telnet sync sequence, which discards data until a data mark arrives. An option subnegotiation could be defined that would be lost this way.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 728 warns that a Telnet sync can discard data while leaving control information intact. An option designed to affect following data could then affect the wrong data after synchronization.

questions: telnet option design problem data mark
how does telnet sync affect options
how can telnet subnegotiation interact with sync
how should telnet options recover after a data mark
subtitle: A warning that Telnet synchronization can discard data needed by an option.

tldr.problem: Telnet's sync sequence discards data up to a data mark, which could leave an option subnegotiation affecting the wrong data.
tldr.mechanism: The memo suggests putting affected data inside the subnegotiation or defining a recovery mechanism after the data mark to cancel an unintended effect.
tldr.outcome: The RFC asks future Telnet option designers to account for this possible interaction; it says no existing option then had the problem.

today: RFC 728 is a design warning about a possible interaction between Telnet synchronization and future options. It says none of the existing options were affected at the time.

sections.title: What Synchronization Discards
sections.content:
The Telnet sync sequence deletes data from the stream until a data mark is encountered. Telnet control functions are not affected by this sequence.

The memo says no existing Telnet options are susceptible at the time of writing, but a future option could have an effect on data that follows its subnegotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: During sync, Telnet discards data up to a special mark, but it keeps control functions. A future option might therefore remain active after its related data is discarded.

sections.title: How an Option Could Affect the Wrong Data
sections.content:
If an option subnegotiation changes how following data is handled, and a sync discards that data before the subnegotiation is processed, the option's effect could apply to later data instead.

The memo gives an example of a subnegotiation requesting that later terminal text use a particular font or receive other special treatment.
sections.plainLanguage: An option could set a mode for data that sync then removes. The mode might remain and affect data that was not meant to use it.

sections.title: Two Possible Design Responses
sections.content:
One possibility is to include the affected data as a parameter inside the subnegotiation. The RFC notes that this does not fit the Telnet design approach and could still cause confusing behavior if a sync occurs.

Another possibility is for an option to define a subnegotiation or other mechanism immediately after a data mark that cancels effects from an earlier subnegotiation. The exact behavior would depend on the option.
sections.plainLanguage: An option can carry its affected data inside its control message, or define a way to undo its effect after a data mark. Each option would need its own recovery behavior.
